summary: This Wikipedia-derived note surveys relations between Tibet and the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), focusing on the religious patron-priest character of ties with Karmapa, Gelug and other Tibetan lamas and the Ming court's titles and invitations. It also covers the scholarly and political dispute over whether Ming China held sovereignty over Tibet, contrasting PRC official and Chinese scholarly claims with views from Wylie, Goldstein, Kolmaš and Sperling, and traces the transition to Qing and Dalai Lama power.
one_line: Overview of Ming dynasty ties with Tibetan Buddhist leaders and the scholarly dispute over whether Tibet was under Ming sovereignty.
key_facts: The Yongle Emperor received Deshin Shekpa, the Karmapa, in Nanjing and did not require him to kowtow like a tributary vassal.
Rolpe Dorje, 4th Karmapa Lama (1340–1383), rejected the Hongwu Emperor's invitation but sent some disciples as envoys to the court in Nanjing.
Je Tsongkhapa (1357–1419), founder of the Gelug school, declined the Yongle Emperor's invitation to the Ming court, citing old age, physical weakness and efforts to build three major monasteries.
In 1415 the Yongle Emperor bestowed the title of "State Teacher" on Tsongkhapa's disciple Chosrje Shākya Yeshes, the same title earlier awarded to the Phagmodrupa ruler of Tibet.

In 1515 the Zhengde Emperor sent the eunuch Liu Yun to invite Mikyö Dorje, 8th Karmapa Lama, to Beijing, but the Karmapa refused and launched a surprise ambush that killed or wounded half of Liu Yun's escort.
The Ming court cut off all relations with the Karmapa hierarchs in 1446, having been unaware that Deshin Shekpa had died in 1415.

Wang Jiawei and Nyima Gyaincain assert that the Ming dynasty had unquestioned sovereignty over Tibet, while Turrell V. Wylie, Melvin C. Goldstein and Helmut Hoffman say the relationship was one of suzerainty with nominal Ming titles.
The official position of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the PRC holds that the Ming granted titles and set up administrative organs over Tibet, including the Ü-Tsang Commanding Office.
An edict of the Hongwu Emperor in 1373 appointed the Tibetan leader Choskunskyabs as General of the Ngari Military and Civil Wanhu Office.
The Wanli Emperor granted the fourth Dalai Lama Yonten Gyatso the title "Master of Vajradhara" and an official seal in 1616, but Yonten Gyatso died before making the journey to Beijing.
Shunzhi Emperor of the Qing invited the fifth Dalai Lama Lozang Gyatso to Beijing in 1652 and treated him as an independent sovereign of Tibet.
Elliot Sperling writes that the idea that Tibet became part of China in the 13th century is "a very recent construction" and that "China's intervening Ming dynasty ... had no control over Tibet."

During the reign of the Jiajing Emperor, Daoism was fully sponsored at court while Tibetan Vajrayana and Chinese Buddhism were ignored or suppressed, and Tibetan lamas discontinued their trips to the Ming court.
China Daily, a CCP-controlled news organization since 1981, stated in a 2008 article that "Tibet has remained under the jurisdiction of the central government of China."

entities.name: Deshin Shekpa
entities.role: Karmapa lama who was induced by Ming court exhortations to visit Nanjing by April 10, 1407, and was honored by the Yongle Emperor

entities.name: Yongle Emperor
entities.role: Ming emperor who showed great deference to Deshin Shekpa and invited Je Tsongkhapa to court

entities.name: Hongwu Emperor
entities.role: Ming emperor who wanted to foster Tibet-China Buddhist links and entrusted monk Zongluo with a mission to Tibet

entities.name: Rolpe Dorje, 4th Karmapa Lama
entities.role: Karmapa lama (1340–1383) who rejected the Hongwu Emperor's invitation

entities.name: Zongluo
entities.role: Buddhist monk and guru of the Hongwu Emperor who headed a religious mission into Tibet in 1378–1382

entities.name: Zhengtong Emperor
entities.role: Ming emperor (r. 1435–1449) who sent an edict to the Karmapa in 1445

entities.name: Je Tsongkhapa
entities.role: Founder of the Gelug school (1357–1419) who declined Ming invitations to visit the court

entities.name: Hou Xian
entities.role: Eunuch leading the 1413 Ming embassy to Tsongkhapa, which was refused

entities.name: Chosrje Shākya Yeshes
entities.role: Disciple of Tsongkhapa sent to Nanjing in 1414 who received the title State Teacher and later a King title from the Xuande Emperor

entities.name: Xuande Emperor
entities.role: Ming emperor (r. 1425–1435) who granted Chosrje Shākya Yeshes the title of King

entities.name: Zhengde Emperor
entities.role: Ming emperor (r. 1505–1521) who sought to host the Karmapa and sent Liu Yun on a failed mission

entities.name: Mikyö Dorje, 8th Karmapa Lama
entities.role: Karmapa lama occupying Lhasa, invited to Beijing in 1515 but refused to leave Tibet

entities.name: Liu Yun
entities.role: Eunuch official of the Palace Chancellery whose 1515 mission to invite the Karmapa failed

entities.name: Liang Chu
entities.role: Grand Secretary who protested the Zhengde Emperor's invitation

entities.name: Jiajing Emperor
entities.role: Ming emperor (1521–1566/1567) under whom relations with Tibet ceased and Daoism was sponsored

entities.name: Yang Tinghe
entities.role: Grand Secretary under Jiajing who sought to break eunuch influence at court

entities.name: Wanli Emperor
entities.role: Ming emperor who granted Yonten Gyatso a title and seal in 1616

entities.name: Yonten Gyatso
entities.role: Fourth Dalai Lama who received the title Master of Vajradhara and an official seal in 1616

entities.name: Choskunskyabs
entities.role: Tibetan leader appointed General of the Ngari Military and Civil Wanhu Office by a Hongwu edict in 1373

entities.name: Li Zicheng
entities.role: Rebel leader whose rebellion brought down the Ming dynasty in 1644

entities.name: Wu Sangui
entities.role: Han Chinese general who helped crush the Shun dynasty

entities.name: Shunzhi Emperor
entities.role: Qing emperor (r. 1644–1661) who invited the fifth Dalai Lama to Beijing in 1652

entities.name: Lozang Gyatso
entities.role: Fifth Dalai Lama (1617–1682) invited to Beijing by the Shunzhi Emperor in 1652

entities.name: Altan Khan
entities.role: Mongol leader whose conversion to the Gelug was interpreted as an attempt to expand his authority

entities.role: Specialist of Indian studies at Indiana University who argued against the claim that Tibet became part of China in the 13th century

entities.name: Turrell V. Wylie
entities.role: Scholar who holds that Ming-Tibet relations were suzerainty with nominal titles

entities.name: Melvin C. Goldstein
entities.role: Scholar who holds that Tibet remained independent outside Ming control

entities.name: Helmut Hoffman
entities.role: Scholar who holds that Ming-Tibet relations were suzerainty

entities.role: Mainland Chinese scholar who asserts Ming unquestioned sovereignty over Tibet
